analysis.one_liner: Ends federal milk price supports and marketing orders, letting states set their own minimum milk prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in House Agriculture and Judiciary subcommittees until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, leaving federal milk price supports and marketing orders in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would shut down the federal programs that keep milk prices up: the government's milk price support, the loans that back processor inventories, and the federal milk marketing orders that set what processors must pay farmers. In their place, it would let any state, or a group of states acting together, set a minimum price for the milk produced within their borders. The practical effect is to shift milk price-setting from Washington to state capitols, ending taxpayer-funded purchases of surplus butter, cheese, and milk powder while likely raising retail milk prices in states that choose to set minimums.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers in states or interstate compacts that choose to set minimum fluid milk prices above the market level, because their buyers would be required to pay more per hundredweight. Taxpayers also benefit, since the federal government would stop buying surplus butter, cheese, and nonfat dry milk to prop up prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Dairy farmers in states that set minimums

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal milk price support program and the recourse loan program for processors, ending federal purchases of cheese, butter, and nonfat dry milk used to hold milk prices up.
Terminates federal milk marketing orders, the Depression-era system that sets minimum prices processors must pay dairy farmers and pools their revenues.
Grants congressional consent for any state or compact of states to establish a minimum price for fluid milk produced in that state or compact, and to regulate milk used for manufacturing.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers in states or compacts that set minimum milk prices would pay more at the store, since a price floor set above the market raises what processors and retailers charge. Dairy farmers in states that do not act would lose the federal price floor and the marketing-order payment rules that now support their incomes.

drawbacks.text: State minimum milk prices would raise retail milk costs for families in participating states; the Northeast Interstate Dairy Compact, the model this bill builds on, was criticized for exactly that effect before Congress let it lapse.
The bill is retroactive on its face, taking effect on January 1, 2001, nearly a year before it was introduced.
Farmers outside any compact would lose the federal price floor entirely, with no replacement, creating a patchwork where milk prices depend on which state a farm sits in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a genuine trade rather than a clean win: it ends taxpayer-funded purchases of surplus dairy products and dismantles a rigid federal pricing apparatus, but it hands pricing power to state compacts that would very likely raise milk prices for consumers in dairy regions. Whether that is a net gain depends on whether you weigh federal subsidy savings and deregulation against higher store prices in participating states. As drafted, it also carries a retroactive effective date that would be hard to apply in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Agriculture and Judiciary committees, split between subcommittees, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Collin Peterson of Minnesota introduced the bill on November 8, 2001, joined by Rep. Richard Pombo of California.
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.

On November 26, 2001, the Agriculture Committee sent it to its Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee, and the USDA was asked for its comments; the next day the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dairy farmers are better off than they would have been under this bill: the federal milk price support and marketing orders it would have repealed stayed in place, and Congress went on to renew dairy support programs in the 2002 farm bill. Consumers and taxpayers did not get the subsidy repeal or the state-compact alternative either — the status quo simply continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dairy farmers, who kept federal supports

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat from Minnesota sponsored the bill with a single Republican cosponsor, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split never got a chance to show itself.

industries.note: The bill repeals the federal price floor and marketing orders that guarantee dairy farm income, but lets states or compacts set their own minimum milk prices instead — farmer gains would come directly out of consumers' pockets in participating states.

Terminating federal marketing orders frees handlers from the rules that dictate what they must pay farmers and how revenues are pooled, but state price mandates could impose new obligations in participating states.
Ending the price support program stops the government from buying surplus butter, cheese, and nonfat dry milk to hold prices up, a cost borne by taxpayers.
